decks.title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence — Part 1: Colonial Aims, Agriculture and Industry
goals: Explain the economic aims of colonial rule and why income grew so slowly
Explain the causes of agricultural stagnation, including land settlement and commercialisation
Explain de-industrialisation and the limits of modern industry in 1947
Use evidence from a case or a table to identify features of the colonial economy

slides.heading: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **why** colonial rule shaped the economy as it did, and the state of **agriculture** and **industry** in 1947.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: aims of colonial rule, low income and slow growth, agriculture, and industry
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: When India became independent in 1947, it inherited an economy shaped by nearly two centuries of colonial rule. To understand the plans and policies that came later, we first need a clear picture of where the country started. In this part we look at the aims of colonial policy, the low level of income, and the state of agriculture and industry.

slides.heading: What colonial policy wanted
slides.body_md: India as a **supplier of raw materials** and a **market** for British manufactures.

visual.alt: Flow of the colonial pattern: Indian raw materials go to British factories, which make finished goods that are sold back in Indian markets
visual.caption: The colonial economic loop

slides.narration: Colonial economic policy served the ruling country, not the colony. India was to send raw materials such as cotton, jute and indigo to British factories, and then buy back the finished goods those factories made. This loop explains almost every feature we will study: stagnant farms, declining crafts, trade tied to Britain, and infrastructure built to move goods to the ports.

slides.heading: Low national income
slides.body_md: The colonial government never measured national income seriously; private scholars did.

headers: Who estimated India's income in colonial times
rows: Early estimate; linked poverty to the drain of wealth
Generally regarded as the most significant

visual.alt: Table of people who estimated colonial India's income: Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, R. C. Desai, and V. K. R. V. Rao, whose estimates are generally regarded as the most significant
visual.caption: The government made no serious estimate; private estimates differ in method.

slides.narration: How poor was colonial India? The government itself made no serious attempt to measure national income. Scholars filled the gap, among them Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras and R. C. Desai. The estimates of V. K. R. V. Rao are generally treated as the most significant. Their methods differed, but all of them pointed to very low income per person.

slides.heading: Very slow growth
slides.body_md: In the first half of the twentieth century, **aggregate real output** grew by **less than 2 per cent** a year, and **output per person** by about **half a per cent**.

headers: First half of the twentieth century

visual.alt: Table: in the first half of the twentieth century aggregate real output grew by less than 2 per cent a year and output per person by about half a per cent
visual.caption: Commonly cited approximate estimates.

slides.narration: Growth was painfully slow. Total output grew by less than two per cent a year in the first half of the twentieth century. Because population was also rising, output per person grew by only about half a per cent a year. At that pace, living standards hardly changed within a lifetime.

slides.heading: Agriculture: the main occupation
slides.body_md: About **85 per cent** of people lived in villages and depended on agriculture, directly or indirectly. Yet the sector **stagnated**: output per acre stayed low.
bullets: Largest sector by people dependent on it
Slow growth of output, low productivity
Some growth of cash crops in a few areas
slides.narration: Agriculture was the backbone of colonial India. Roughly eighty five out of every hundred people lived in villages and depended on farming in some way. But this huge sector was stagnant. Output per acre stayed low, and the little growth that took place came from bringing more land under the plough, not from better methods.

slides.heading: Land settlement: who got the surplus?
slides.body_md: Under the **zamindari** system, landlords collected rent and paid fixed revenue to the state.

nodes.label: Zamindar pays fixed revenue to the colonial state
Little left for investment in land

visual.alt: Flow of the zamindari arrangement: the cultivator pays rent to the zamindar, the zamindar pays fixed revenue to the colonial state, and little is left to invest in the land
visual.caption: Who got the surplus?

slides.narration: Why did farming stagnate? Start with the land settlement. In large areas, especially under the permanent settlement in Bengal, zamindars collected rent from the cultivators and paid a fixed revenue to the colonial government. The zamindar kept the difference, so the surplus went to him, not to the tiller. Few zamindars invested in improving the land, and the cultivator had neither the means nor the reason to do so.

slides.heading: Quick check: revenue terms
slides.body_md: A zamindar must pay a fixed revenue by a fixed date, and the crop fails. What is he likely to do?
slides.narration: Think about the pressure a fixed deadline creates when the harvest fails. Whose burden does it become?

slides.heading: Other causes of stagnation
slides.body_md: Rent pressure, **low technology** and **poor irrigation** worked together.

rows: Rent went to landlords who seldom improved the land
Fixed sums by fixed dates, even in bad years
Wooden ploughs, old seeds, little fertiliser
Most land depended on rain; floods unchecked

visual.alt: Table of four causes of agricultural stagnation: the zamindari land settlement, harsh revenue terms, low technology and poor irrigation, with how each held output back

slides.narration: Land settlement was not the only problem. The terms of revenue were harsh: a fixed sum had to be paid by a fixed date, whatever the harvest. Technology was backward, with wooden ploughs, old seeds and very little fertiliser. And most fields depended on the monsoon, because investment in irrigation and flood control was small. Together these kept yields low.

slides.heading: Commercialisation of agriculture
slides.body_md: Some farmers shifted from **food crops** to **cash crops** for British industry.

nodes.label: Cash crops for British industry (indigo, jute, cotton)

visual.alt: Flow of commercialisation: farmers shift from food crops to cash crops for British industry; gains go to traders, moneylenders and exporters, while cultivators stay poor and grow less food
visual.caption: Commercialisation without prosperity

slides.narration: In some regions farmers began growing cash crops such as indigo, jute and cotton, often to feed British mills. This is called commercialisation of agriculture. It raised the output of these crops in a few areas, but the gains went mostly to traders, moneylenders and exporters. Most cultivators stayed poor and indebted, and growing less food made families more exposed to famine.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a case
slides.body_md: An imagined account describes a village in 1900. Find the features of colonial agriculture it shows.
bullets: Step 1 — Underline each **clue** in the passage.
Step 2 — Name the **feature** it shows, using the exact term.
Step 3 — Link the feature to its **effect** on output or on the cultivator.

rows: Half the crop goes as rent to the landlord's agent
The village grows indigo for a European planter
One canal, dry most of the year; fields wait for rain
The same wooden plough as the grandfather

visual.alt: Table linking four clues in an imagined account to features of colonial agriculture: rent to the landlord's agent is zamindari, indigo for a planter is commercialisation, a dry canal is poor irrigation, an old wooden plough is low technology
visual.caption: Imagined village; quote the clue, then name the feature.

slides.narration: Case questions reward precise matching. Here is an imagined village. Half the crop goes as rent to the landlord's agent, so that is the zamindari settlement. Indigo grown for a European planter shows commercialisation. A canal that stays dry shows poor irrigation, and the grandfather's wooden plough shows low technology. Quote the clue, name the feature, and add its effect.

slides.heading: Quick check: causes of stagnation
slides.body_md: Which one was **NOT** a cause of agricultural stagnation in colonial India?
slides.narration: One of these options belongs to a much later period of Indian farming. Spot it.

slides.heading: Industry: de-industrialisation
slides.body_md: Traditional **handicrafts declined**, and **modern industry did not grow** enough to replace them.

nodes.label: Cheap machine-made British cloth enters at low duty
Few modern factories to absorb them
More pressure on land and more unemployment

visual.alt: Flow of de-industrialisation: cheap British cloth enters at low duty, handicrafts lose their market, artisans lose work, few factories absorb them, so pressure on land and unemployment rise
visual.caption: De-industrialisation in five steps

slides.narration: Now industry. India was once famous for its handicrafts, especially fine cotton and silk textiles. Under colonial rule, cheap machine-made cloth from British mills entered the country at low duty and took away the craftsmen's market. Artisans lost their work, and very few modern factories came up to employ them. This double process, decline without replacement, is called de-industrialisation.

slides.heading: The two-fold motive
columns:
**Raw materials**

Cheap cotton, jute, indigo and silk for Britain's growing factories.

**Market**

A vast Indian market for British cloth and other manufactured goods.

rows: Cheap raw materials for British industry
India exported cotton, jute, indigo, silk
A large market for British finished goods
Indian crafts were undersold at home

visual.alt: Table of the two-fold motive of colonial industrial policy: cheap raw materials for British industry, and a market for British finished goods, with what each meant for India

slides.narration: Why did colonial policy allow, and even encourage, the decline of Indian crafts? There were two motives. First, India was to be a source of cheap raw materials for Britain's expanding industries. Second, India was to be a large market for the finished goods those industries produced. Thriving Indian crafts would have competed with both aims.

slides.heading: Quick check: a weaver's loss
slides.body_md: An imagined weaver family in Bengal loses its customers in the 1880s. Why?
slides.narration: Ask which change made the weaver's cloth look expensive to buyers.

slides.heading: Modern industry: a slow start
slides.body_md: Modern factories came up from the **second half of the nineteenth century**, but growth stayed slow.

rows: Came up later, after the Second World War

visual.alt: Table of modern industries in colonial India: cotton mills in western India, mainly Indian-owned; jute mills in Bengal, mainly foreign-owned; iron and steel with TISCO in 1907; sugar, cement and paper later
visual.caption: Approximate, commonly cited pattern.

slides.narration: Modern industry did begin, but slowly. Cotton textile mills came up in western India, mostly owned by Indians. Jute mills grew around Bengal, mostly owned by foreigners. The Tata Iron and Steel Company was incorporated in nineteen hundred and seven. Sugar, cement and paper factories followed later. Even so, industry's share of national output remained small.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: measuring a craftsman's loss
slides.body_md: An imagined weaver earned ₹240 a year before mill cloth reached his town and ₹150 after. Find the percentage fall.
bullets: Step 2 — Percentage fall = fall ÷ original × 100 = 37.5%.
Step 3 — Interpret: a loss of more than a third of income pushes the family towards farm labour or debt.

visual.alt: Table of a worked example: an imagined weaver's income falls from 240 to 150 rupees a year, a fall of 90 rupees, which is 37.5 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Let us put a number on de-industrialisation for one imagined weaver. His income fell from two hundred and forty rupees a year to one hundred and fifty. The fall is ninety rupees. Divide by the original income and multiply by one hundred, and you get thirty seven and a half per cent. Always finish with the meaning: such a loss pushed artisans back to the land.

slides.heading: Quick check: your turn
slides.body_md: Try the percentage fall for the weaver in the practice question.
slides.narration: Use the same two steps: find the fall, then divide by the original income and multiply by one hundred.

slides.heading: The weak base of industry
slides.body_md: Almost **no capital goods industry**, and a **small public sector**.

nodes.label: New industry slow and costly to start
Small public sector: railways, power, communication, ports

visual.alt: Flow: hardly any capital goods industry meant machines had to be imported, so new industry was slow and costly; the public sector was small, limited to railways, power, communication and ports
visual.caption: The weak base of industry

slides.narration: Two more gaps mattered. India had hardly any capital goods industry, the industry that makes machines and machine tools. So every new factory needed imported machinery, which made industrial growth slow and costly. The public sector was also small, limited mainly to railways, power, communication, ports and a few departmental undertakings.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Raw materials out, British goods in
Low; growth under 2 per cent a year, per head about half a per cent
Main occupation, but stagnant: zamindari, low technology, little irrigation
Handicrafts declined; few modern mills; no capital goods base

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: colonial aims, low income and slow growth, stagnant agriculture and weak industry in 1947

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Colonial policy made India a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods. Income was low and grew very slowly. Agriculture employed most people but stagnated because of the zamindari system, harsh revenue terms, poor technology and little irrigation. Handicrafts declined, modern industry stayed small, and there was almost no capital goods base.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define **de-industrialisation** with both halves: crafts declined **and** modern industry did not replace them.
For stagnation, give the **cause and its effect**: zamindari → rent to landlords → no investment.
Commercialisation is **not** prosperity: say who gained (traders, exporters) and who did not.
Quote figures as **approximate**: growth under 2 per cent a year, per head about half a per cent.
Jute mills: Bengal, mainly foreign-owned; cotton mills: western India, mainly Indian-owned.
slides.narration: A few tips for the board paper. When you define de-industrialisation, write both halves: the decline of crafts and the failure of modern industry to replace them. For every cause of stagnation, add its effect. Never call commercialisation a success without saying who gained. Quote figures as approximate. And remember which region and which owners went with cotton and jute mills.

decks.title: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence — Part 2: Trade, People and Infrastructure
goals: Describe the composition and direction of foreign trade and explain the drain of the export surplus
Describe the demographic condition, including the significance of 1921
Interpret the occupational structure and its regional variation
Appraise colonial infrastructure in a balanced way

slides.heading: Trade, People and Infrastructure in 1947
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **foreign trade**, **population**, **occupations** and **infrastructure**, then the overall picture.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: foreign trade, demographic condition, occupational structure, infrastructure and the overall picture
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we look outward and then at the people. How did India trade with the world, and who gained from it? What did population, literacy and health look like? Where did people work? And what kind of roads, railways and communications did independent India inherit?

slides.heading: Composition of foreign trade
slides.body_md: India became an **exporter of primary products** and an **importer of finished goods**.

visual.alt: Table of the composition of colonial India's trade: exports were mainly primary products such as raw cotton, silk, wool, jute, indigo and sugar; imports were mainly finished cloth, light machinery and iron goods

slides.narration: Look at what crossed the ports. India sent out primary products: raw cotton, raw silk, wool, jute, indigo and sugar. It brought in finished consumer goods such as cotton, silk and woollen cloth, along with light machinery from British factories. This is exactly the colonial loop from Part 1, now seen at the docks.

slides.heading: Direction of trade and the Suez Canal
slides.body_md: Britain kept a **monopoly**: more than half of India's trade was with Britain.

nodes.label: British control of exports and imports
More than half of trade with Britain
Rest mainly with China, Ceylon, Persia
Suez Canal (1869) cuts freight time and cost

visual.alt: Flow: British control of trade, more than half of it with Britain, the rest mainly with China, Ceylon and Persia, and the Suez Canal of 1869 cutting freight time and cost
visual.caption: Direction of trade

slides.narration: Britain controlled India's exports and imports, so more than half of all trade went to or came from Britain. The rest was mainly with China, Ceylon and Persia. The opening of the Suez Canal in eighteen sixty nine shortened the sea route between Britain and India, making freight cheaper and faster and tightening this control.

slides.heading: Quick check: the canal
slides.body_md: How did the opening of the Suez Canal affect India's trade?
slides.narration: Think about distance, cost, and whose goods could now move more cheaply.

slides.heading: A surplus that became a drain
slides.body_md: Exports exceeded imports, but the **surplus left the country**.

nodes.label: Pays for colonial office in Britain
Pays for wars and invisible imports
No gold or silver comes in
Shortages of grain, cloth, kerosene at home

visual.alt: Flow of the drain: the export surplus pays for the colonial office in Britain, wars and invisible imports, no gold or silver comes in, and shortages of grain, cloth and kerosene persist
visual.caption: Why a surplus became a drain

slides.narration: India usually exported more than it imported, so it earned an export surplus. Normally that would add to a country's wealth. But this surplus paid for the colonial government's office in Britain, for wars, and for invisible imports such as shipping and insurance. No gold or silver flowed in, and shortages of grain, cloth and kerosene continued. That is why it is called a drain of wealth.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: calculating and interpreting a surplus
slides.body_md: An imagined district port records exports of ₹74 lakh and imports of ₹51 lakh in a year, and no bullion arrives.
bullets: Step 1 — Export surplus = exports − imports = 74 − 51 = ₹23 lakh.
Step 2 — Ask where it went: the colonial establishment, wars, invisible imports.
Step 3 — Conclude: a surplus with no inflow of wealth is a **drain**.

rows: Surplus sent abroad, no bullion in → drain

visual.alt: Table of a worked example: an imagined district port exports 74 and imports 51 lakh rupees of goods, an export surplus of 23, which is interpreted as a drain because no bullion came in
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Here is how to handle a trade question. Subtract imports from exports to find the surplus: seventy four minus fifty one gives twenty three lakh rupees. Then interpret it. If no gold or silver came in, the surplus was used up abroad. The marks are in the second step: naming where the surplus went and calling it a drain.

slides.heading: Population: 1921, the great divide
slides.body_md: The first census was in **1881**. Before **1921**, growth was slow and uneven; after it, steady.

visual.alt: Schematic line chart of birth and death rates from 1881 to 1951: before 1921 both are high and close, so population grows slowly; after 1921 the death rate falls while the birth rate stays high, so population grows steadily
visual.caption: Schematic only (shapes, not actual data): 1921 separates the first and second stages.

slides.narration: The first census was taken in eighteen eighty one. Until nineteen twenty one, both birth and death rates were high, so population grew slowly and unevenly: the first stage of the demographic transition. After nineteen twenty one the death rate began to fall while the birth rate stayed high, so population grew steadily. That is why nineteen twenty one is called the year of the great divide. The chart shows shapes only, not exact data.

slides.heading: Quick check: which stage?
slides.body_md: A region has a birth rate of 46 and a death rate of 44 per thousand. How is its population changing?
slides.narration: Subtract the death rate from the birth rate. Is that a small or a large gap?

slides.heading: The quality of life
slides.body_md: Low literacy, short lives and very high infant mortality.

visual.alt: Table of approximate demographic indicators around 1947: overall literacy below 16 per cent, female literacy about 7 per cent, life expectancy about 32 years, infant mortality over 200 per thousand live births
visual.caption: Commonly cited approximate values.

slides.narration: The social indicators were grim. Fewer than one in six people could read and write, and among women only about seven in a hundred. Life expectancy at birth was only about thirty two years. Infant mortality was over two hundred per thousand live births. Public health facilities were scarce, and water borne and air borne diseases spread widely. Poverty was extensive.

slides.narration: Where did people work? Agriculture employed the largest share of the workforce, about seventy to seventy five per cent. Manufacturing employed only about ten per cent, and services about fifteen to twenty per cent. An economy where three out of four workers are on the land, with low productivity, is a poor, agrarian economy.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a district's workforce
slides.body_md: An imagined district has 40,000 workers, 29,200 of them in agriculture. Find the share and compare it with India.
bullets: Step 2 — Compare: inside the all-India range of about 70–75 per cent.
Step 3 — Conclude: a typical agrarian district of the time.

rows: Inside the all-India range of 70–75 per cent

visual.alt: Table of a worked example: 29,200 of 40,000 workers in agriculture gives a share of 73 per cent, inside the all-India range of 70 to 75 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Data questions often ask you to compute a share and compare. Divide the agricultural workers by all workers and multiply by one hundred: here that gives seventy three per cent. Then compare with the all India range of seventy to seventy five per cent and draw a conclusion: this imagined district is typical of its time.

slides.heading: Quick check: a province
slides.body_md: Find the share of agriculture in the workforce of an imagined province.
slides.narration: Divide, multiply by one hundred, and check whether your answer looks reasonable for that period.

slides.heading: Growing regional variation
slides.body_md: The share of agriculture **fell slightly** in some regions and **rose** in others.

headers: Share of agriculture in the workforce
rows: Parts of the Madras, Bombay and Bengal presidencies

visual.alt: Table of the regional pattern: in parts of the Madras, Bombay and Bengal presidencies the share of agriculture in the workforce fell slightly, while in Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab it rose
visual.caption: Growing regional variation.

slides.narration: The national figures hide differences between regions. In parts of the Madras, Bombay and Bengal presidencies, the share of workers in agriculture fell slightly as some industry and services grew. In regions such as Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab, the share actually rose. So regional variation in the occupational structure was widening.

slides.heading: Railways: a mixed legacy
columns:
**Gains**

Long-distance travel; geographical and cultural barriers broken; wider markets.

**Costs**

Built for administration and export trade; carried British goods inland; aided commercialisation more than the cultivator.

rows: Built to serve administration and export trade
Carried British goods inland, hurting crafts
Helped commercialisation more than the cultivator

visual.alt: Two-column table of the railways: gains were long-distance travel, breaking geographical and cultural barriers and wider markets; costs were a colonial purpose, carrying British goods inland and favouring commercialisation over the cultivator

slides.narration: The railways, which began carrying passengers in eighteen fifty three, are the best known colonial infrastructure. They made long distance travel possible and helped break geographical and cultural barriers. But their routes were planned to move raw materials to the ports and British goods into the interior, which hurt crafts. A balanced answer gives both sides.

slides.heading: Roads, waterways, posts and telegraph
slides.body_md: Built mainly for **colonial purposes**; coverage of villages stayed poor.

rows: Moving troops; linking the interior to railway stations and ports
Some, like a coastal canal in Orissa, were uneconomical

visual.alt: Table of other colonial infrastructure: roads for troops and links to stations and ports, with few all-weather village roads; waterways, some uneconomical; posts, inadequate; and the electric telegraph, mainly for law and order

slides.narration: Roads were built mainly to move troops and to link the interior to railway stations and ports, so most villages lacked all weather roads. Some inland waterways, such as a coastal canal in Orissa, turned out to be uneconomical. Posts served the public but remained inadequate. The electric telegraph was expanded mainly to help maintain law and order.

slides.body_md: Which was a **positive** effect of the railways in colonial India?
slides.narration: Three of these options are claims the evidence does not support. Find the one that does hold.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: planning a five-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: "Critically appraise the impact of British rule on the Indian economy."
bullets: Step 1 — Plan five areas: agriculture, industry, trade, demography, infrastructure.
Step 2 — One **key term** each: zamindari, de-industrialisation, drain, 1921, railways.
Step 3 — Add one fact or effect to each point.
Step 4 — "Critically appraise" needs a **conclusion**: weak and stagnant economy, with a usable infrastructure base.

nodes.label: Plan five areas or five points
One bold key term per point
Add one fact or example each
End with a judgement if asked to evaluate

visual.alt: Flow for structuring a five-mark answer: read the command word, plan five points, put one key term in bold per point, add a fact or example to each, and end with a judgement when asked to evaluate
visual.caption: A five-mark plan

slides.narration: Long answers in this chapter are easy to plan if you use the five areas as your five points. Give each point one key term and one fact. Watch the command word: appraise or evaluate means you must end with a judgement, such as a stagnant economy that nevertheless left a base of railways and ports.

sections.heading: 1. Colonial aims and low level of development
sections.body_md:
Colonial economic policy aimed to make India a **supplier of raw materials** to British industry and a **market for British finished goods**. Development of the Indian economy was not its concern.

**National income:** the colonial government made no serious estimate. Private estimates were made by **Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V. K. R. V. Rao** and **R. C. Desai**; Rao's are generally regarded as the most significant.

**Growth (first half of the twentieth century, approximate):** aggregate real output under **2 per cent** a year; output per person about **0.5 per cent** a year.

key_terms.definition_md: An economy run to serve the interests of the ruling country rather than its own people.
National income divided by population; an average income per person.

sections.heading: 2. Agriculture: largest and stagnant
sections.body_md:
About **85 per cent** of people lived in villages and depended on agriculture. Output grew slowly and productivity was low.

**Causes of stagnation:**
1. **Land settlement** — under **zamindari** (permanent settlement in Bengal), zamindars collected rent and paid fixed revenue; the surplus went to them, and few invested in the land.
2. **Revenue terms** — fixed sums by fixed dates, even when crops failed; tenants were squeezed.
3. **Low technology** — old tools, little fertiliser.
4. **Poor irrigation and flood control.**
5. **Commercialisation** — a shift to cash crops (indigo, jute, cotton) for British industry, which raised output in a few areas but enriched traders and exporters more than cultivators.

key_terms.definition_md: A land settlement in which landlords collected rent from cultivators and paid revenue to the state.
Growing crops for sale in the market (cash crops) rather than for the family's own use.
Little or no growth over a long period.

sections.heading: 3. Industry: decline of crafts, slow modern growth
sections.body_md:
**De-industrialisation:** traditional handicrafts declined and modern industry did not replace them. Cheap machine-made British goods, imported at low duty, took the craftsmen's market; artisans were pushed into farming or unemployment.

**Two-fold motive:** cheap raw materials for Britain, and a large market for British manufactures.

**Modern industry:** cotton mills in western India (mainly Indian-owned) and jute mills in Bengal (mainly foreign-owned) from the second half of the nineteenth century; **TISCO, 1907**; sugar, cement and paper later. Industry's share of output stayed small.

**Weak base:** almost **no capital goods industry**; the **public sector** was limited to railways, power, communication, ports and some departmental undertakings.

key_terms.definition_md: The decline of existing industries without new industries taking their place.
Machines and tools used to produce other goods.

sections.heading: 4. Foreign trade and the drain
sections.body_md:
**Composition:** exporter of **primary products** (raw cotton, raw silk, wool, jute, indigo, sugar); importer of **finished goods** (cloth, light machinery).

**Direction:** a British **monopoly** — more than half of India's trade was with Britain; the rest mainly with China, Ceylon and Persia. The **Suez Canal (1869)** cut the time and cost of shipping.

**Export surplus and drain:** exports exceeded imports, but the surplus paid for the colonial office in Britain, wars and invisible imports. No gold or silver came in, and grain, cloth and kerosene were scarce at home.

key_terms.definition_md: The excess of the value of exports over the value of imports.
The transfer of India's surplus to Britain without any return to India.

sections.heading: 5. Demographic condition
sections.body_md:
The **first census** was taken in **1881**. Until **1921**, birth and death rates were both high and growth was slow (first stage of the demographic transition). After 1921 the death rate fell while the birth rate stayed high, so population grew steadily: **1921 is the year of the great divide**.

**Approximate indicators:** literacy under **16 per cent** (women about **7 per cent**); life expectancy about **32 years**; infant mortality **over 200** per thousand. Public health facilities were scarce; diseases and famines were frequent; poverty was widespread.

key_terms.definition_md: The change from high birth and death rates to low ones as a country develops.
Deaths of infants under one year per thousand live births.
The average number of years a newborn is expected to live.

sections.heading: 6. Occupational structure
sections.body_md:
**Occupational structure** is the distribution of the workforce across sectors. Around 1947, approximately: **agriculture 70–75 per cent**, **manufacturing about 10 per cent**, **services 15–20 per cent**.

**Regional variation:** the share of agriculture fell slightly in parts of the Madras, Bombay and Bengal presidencies, but rose in Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab.

sections.heading: 7. Infrastructure: a mixed legacy
sections.body_md:
**Railways** (passenger service from **1853**): long-distance travel, broke geographical and cultural barriers, wider markets; but built for administration and export trade, carried British goods inland and aided commercialisation.

**Roads** served troops and linked the interior to stations and ports; most villages had no all-weather roads. **Inland waterways** were developed, but some (like a coastal canal in Orissa) were uneconomical. **Posts** remained inadequate; the **electric telegraph** served mainly law and order.

**Overall:** independent India inherited a poor, stagnant economy, with a usable but colonially shaped base of infrastructure.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Defining de-industrialisation as "no industry": it is the **decline of crafts without replacement** by modern industry.
- Calling commercialisation a gain for farmers: the gains went mainly to **traders and exporters**.
- Treating the export surplus as wealth: it was a **drain**.
- Writing 1881 as the great divide: **1881** = first census; **1921** = great divide.
- Giving precise figures as exact: say **about 32 years**, **under 16 per cent**, **70–75 per cent**.
- One-sided infrastructure answers: give **gains and costs**, then judge.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two points, or a definition and a reason (30–50 words).
- 3 marks: three distinct points (50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five points with key terms and facts (80–120 words); "evaluate" needs a judgement.
- Case-based: quote the clue from the passage, then name the feature.

questions.stem_md: The main economic aim of British colonial policy in India was to

options.text_md: build a strong capital goods industry in India
turn India into a supplier of raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods
make India self-reliant in food and machinery
raise the living standards of Indian farmers through land reform

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** turn India into a supplier of raw materials and a market for British manufactured goods. Colonial policy served the interests of the ruling country: raw materials flowed to British factories and their finished goods were sold back in India. Building Indian heavy industry, self-reliance and land reform were never its goals.

questions.stem_md: Whose estimates of India's national and per capita income during the colonial period are generally regarded as the most significant?

options.text_md: Adam Smith
J. M. Keynes
Alfred Marshall
V. K. R. V. Rao

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** V. K. R. V. Rao. Several Indian and British scholars estimated India's income in colonial times; the estimates of V. K. R. V. Rao are usually treated as the most important. The other three are economists who did not estimate Indian national income.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the growth of India's economy in the first half of the twentieth century?

options.text_md: Aggregate real output grew by less than 2 per cent a year and per capita output by about half a per cent
Output grew by about 8 per cent a year, mainly because of railways
Output fell every year from 1900 to 1947
Per capita output grew faster than in Britain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Aggregate real output grew by less than 2 per cent a year and per capita output by about half a per cent. Estimates for that period show very slow growth: under 2 per cent a year for total output and only about half a per cent per head, since population also grew. There was neither a boom nor a continuous fall.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The colonial government made no serious effort to measure India's national and per capita income.

**Reason (R):** Individual scholars such as Dadabhai Naoroji and William Digby made estimates of India's income during the colonial period.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is true: the government did not measure national income seriously, and private estimates differ in method and results. R is also true, but it does not explain A; it only says who filled the gap.

questions.stem_md: On the eve of independence, roughly what share of India's population depended on agriculture, directly or indirectly, for a living?

options.text_md: About 25 per cent
About 50 per cent
About 85 per cent
About 10 per cent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** About 85 per cent. Most Indians lived in villages and depended on farming: the usual estimate is about 85 per cent of the population. The other figures are far too low for an agrarian colonial economy.

questions.stem_md: Under the zamindari system in parts of colonial India, the zamindars

options.text_md: were small farmers who owned and tilled their own land
were government officers paid a fixed salary to build irrigation
collected rent from cultivators but rarely invested in improving the land
bought crops from farmers at a guaranteed support price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** collected rent from cultivators but rarely invested in improving the land. The land revenue arrangement placed zamindars between the state and the tiller. Their interest lay in collecting as much rent as possible, so little was spent on improving land. They were not tillers, salaried officers or crop buyers.

questions.stem_md: **Commercialisation of agriculture** in colonial India refers to

options.text_md: a shift by some farmers from food crops to cash crops such as indigo, cotton and jute
the use of tractors and combine harvesters on most farms
the government buying all food grains at fixed prices
the replacement of farming by factory work in villages

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a shift by some farmers from food crops to cash crops such as indigo, cotton and jute. Some areas moved from food grains to crops sold for cash, largely to supply British industry. This did not bring mechanisation or prosperity to most farmers, and farming remained the main occupation.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following was **NOT** a cause of the stagnation of agriculture under colonial rule?

options.text_md: Lack of investment in irrigation and flood control
The burden of rent and revenue on cultivators
Low levels of technology on most farms
A widespread use of chemical fertilisers and high-yielding seeds

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A widespread use of chemical fertilisers and high-yielding seeds. Fertilisers and high-yielding seeds spread only after independence (the Green Revolution of the 1960s). Poor irrigation, heavy rent and revenue demands and backward technology were real causes of colonial stagnation.

questions.stem_md: An imagined zamindar must deposit a fixed sum of revenue by a set date each year or lose his rights. A drought ruins the crop. What is he most likely to do?

options.text_md: Cancel the rent for the year and invest in a canal
Press the cultivators hard for rent anyway, worsening their distress
Ask the government for a subsidy on fertilisers
Switch the village to factory production

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Press the cultivators hard for rent anyway, worsening their distress. Fixed revenue deadlines left no room for bad years, so rent was extracted even when harvests failed, adding to tenants' misery. Waiving rent and building canals was rare, fertiliser subsidies did not exist, and a village cannot simply turn industrial.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In some regions, colonial agriculture showed higher yields of cash crops in particular years.

**Reason (R):** Commercialisation of agriculture made most Indian farmers prosperous.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: there were pockets of higher cash-crop output. R is false: the gains went largely to traders, moneylenders and British industry, while most cultivators stayed poor and indebted.

questions.stem_md: True or false? By 1947 most of India's farmland was irrigated by canals built under colonial rule.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Most farmland still depended on rainfall; investment in irrigation and flood control was very limited, which kept yields low.

questions.stem_md: Under the permanent settlement in Bengal, the profits from agriculture went mainly to the ___ rather than to the cultivators.
questions.solution_md: The zamindars (landlords) collected the rent and kept the surplus; the cultivators were left with little.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons for the low productivity of Indian agriculture under colonial rule.
questions.solution_md: One institutional reason and one technical reason, each explained in a line.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **land settlement system** (zamindari) let landlords take most of the surplus as rent, so neither they nor tenants invested in the land.
2. **Backward technology** and very little **irrigation**, fertiliser or flood control kept yields low.

questions.stem_md: Why did the commercialisation of agriculture not make most Indian farmers better off?
questions.solution_md: Link the cash crop to who captured its value, and add one cost to farmers.

answer.model_answer_md: Farmers were pushed to grow **cash crops for British industry**, but the **prices and profits** were taken largely by **traders, moneylenders** and exporters. Growing less food also left many families **exposed to famine** and debt.

marking_scheme.step: Gains captured by traders or exporters

questions.stem_md: Explain three features of Indian agriculture on the eve of independence.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct features: dependence, stagnation with causes, commercialisation with its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Main occupation:** most of the population lived in villages and depended on farming.
2. **Stagnation:** output per acre stayed low because of the **zamindari** system, rent pressure and **little irrigation or technology**.
3. **Commercialisation:** some regions grew **cash crops** (indigo, jute, cotton) for British industry, but **cultivators gained little** and food security weakened.

questions.stem_md: "Indian agriculture under colonial rule was both the largest and the most stagnant sector." Explain this statement with reasons.
questions.solution_md: One point on size, then four causes of stagnation, each explained briefly.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Largest:** about **85 per cent** of the people depended on farming, and about **seven in ten** workers were cultivators or labourers.
2. **Land settlement:** under **zamindari**, rent went to landlords who **seldom invested**; fixed revenue deadlines squeezed tenants even in bad years.
3. **Low technology:** wooden ploughs, **little fertiliser** and old methods kept yields low.
4. **Poor irrigation:** most land was **rain-fed**; flood control and canals were neglected.
5. **Commercialisation:** cash crops for British industry raised output in **some pockets**, but profits went to traders and exporters, so the sector as a whole **stagnated**.

marking_scheme.step: Size: dependence of people and workers

questions.stem_md: The decline of India's handicraft industries under colonial rule is described as

options.text_md: de-industrialisation
import substitution
liberalisation
disinvestment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** de-industrialisation. The fall of traditional crafts without modern industry taking their place is called de-industrialisation. Import substitution, liberalisation and disinvestment are post-independence policy terms.

questions.stem_md: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was incorporated in the year
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1907. TISCO was incorporated in 1907. The year 1853 is linked with the first passenger train, 1869 with the opening of the Suez Canal, and 1921 with the demographic divide.

questions.stem_md: Which pair correctly matches a modern industry of colonial India with the region where it was concentrated?

options.text_md: Cotton textile mills: Assam
Jute mills: Gujarat
Jute mills: Bengal
Cotton textile mills: Bengal only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Jute mills: Bengal. Jute mills came up mainly around Bengal (and were largely foreign-owned); cotton mills were concentrated in western India, in present-day Maharashtra and Gujarat, and were mainly Indian-owned.

questions.stem_md: Why is the near-absence of a **capital goods industry** in 1947 regarded as a serious weakness?

options.text_md: Capital goods are bought directly by households for consumption
It meant India had no cotton or jute mills at all
It made agricultural output rise too quickly
Without home-made machine tools and machinery, India had to import the means to build any new industry

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Without home-made machine tools and machinery, India had to import the means to build any new industry. Capital goods (machines that make other goods) are the base of industrial growth; lacking them, the country depended on imports for every new factory. Households do not buy capital goods, cotton and jute mills did exist, and agriculture was stagnant.

questions.stem_md: An imagined weaver family in a Bengal village loses its customers in the 1880s. Which colonial-era change best explains this?

options.text_md: The government raised the price of imported cloth with high tariffs
Indian mills made only capital goods
Railways were banned from carrying cloth
Cheap machine-made cloth from British mills flooded Indian markets

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Cheap machine-made cloth from British mills flooded Indian markets. Machine-made British cloth was cheaper and entered India duty-free or at low duty, so hand-woven cloth lost its market. India did not protect its weavers with high tariffs, its mills made consumer goods, and railways actually helped imported cloth reach villages.

questions.stem_md: On the eve of independence, the public sector in India was

options.text_md: the largest employer, running most factories
responsible for most steel and cement production
small, and limited mainly to railways, power, communication, ports and some departmental undertakings
absent altogether

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** small, and limited mainly to railways, power, communication, ports and some departmental undertakings. Government enterprise was confined to a few areas such as railways, power generation, communications and ports. It did not run most factories, steel was private (TISCO), and it was not absent.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** De-industrialisation added to unemployment in colonial India.

**Reason (R):** As handicrafts declined, few modern factories came up to absorb the artisans who lost their work.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: artisans thrown out of work by the collapse of crafts found no new industrial jobs, so many fell back on farming or became unemployed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** By 1947 India had a well-developed machine tools and heavy engineering industry.

**Reason (R):** The growth of the industrial sector during colonial rule was very slow and its share in output remained small.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: there was hardly any capital goods base, only a few beginnings. R is true: industry grew slowly and contributed little to national output.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under colonial rule, India's traditional handicrafts declined without a matching rise of modern industry.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** This two-sided outcome is what de-industrialisation means: crafts fell, and modern industry was too small to replace them.

questions.stem_md: An imagined weaver earned ₹240 a year before machine-made cloth reached his town and ₹150 a year after. By what percentage did his income fall?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Fall = 240 − 150 = 90.
Step 2: Percentage fall = 90 ÷ 240 × 100 = 37.5 per cent.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by de-industrialisation? Give one reason for it in colonial India.
questions.solution_md: A definition plus one cause.

answer.model_answer_md: **De-industrialisation** is the decline of a country's existing industries without new ones taking their place. In India, **cheap machine-made goods from Britain**, imported at low duties, destroyed the market for **handicrafts**.

questions.stem_md: Explain the two-fold motive behind the colonial policy of de-industrialising India.
questions.solution_md: Two motives: raw materials in, finished goods out.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. To obtain **cheap raw materials** from India for the expanding **industries of Britain**.
2. To use India as a large **market for British finished goods**, so that British industry could keep growing.

questions.stem_md: Explain three limitations of the modern industrial sector in India in 1947.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct limitations, each with a brief explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Slow growth:** a few cotton and jute mills, steel (TISCO, 1907) and later sugar, cement and paper; industry's **share of output stayed small**.
2. **No capital goods base:** machines had to be **imported**, so new industry was hard to start.
3. **Uneven and narrow:** factories were confined to a **few regions**, and the **public sector** was limited to railways, ports, power and communication.

marking_scheme.step: Regional concentration or small public sector

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the state of Indian industry on the eve of independence.
questions.solution_md: Four features with evidence, ending in a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Handicrafts declined:** cheap British machine cloth and low import duties destroyed markets of weavers and artisans (**de-industrialisation**).
2. **Few modern industries:** cotton mills in western India (mostly Indian-owned) and jute mills in Bengal (mostly foreign-owned) from the second half of the nineteenth century; **TISCO in 1907**; sugar, cement and paper later.
3. **No capital goods sector:** almost no machine tools, so growth depended on imports.
4. **Small share and slow growth:** industry contributed little to national output.
5. **Limited public sector:** confined to railways, power, communication and ports. **Judgement:** a weak, narrow base that independent India had to rebuild through planning.

marking_scheme.step: Decline of handicrafts and its cause
Modern industries named with region or ownership
Small share or small public sector

questions.stem_md: In colonial times India mainly **exported**

options.text_md: machinery and machine tools
primary products such as raw cotton, raw silk, jute, indigo and sugar
finished woollen and silk garments to Britain
steel and heavy chemicals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** primary products such as raw cotton, raw silk, jute, indigo and sugar. India supplied raw materials and other primary products. It imported finished goods such as cloth and light machinery from British factories; it had no large steel or chemical exports.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about India's foreign trade under colonial rule is correct?

options.text_md: Britain controlled India's trade, and more than half of it was with Britain
Most of India's trade was with the United States
India had a large import surplus every year
India traded freely with every country on equal terms

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Britain controlled India's trade, and more than half of it was with Britain. Through its control of exports and imports, Britain kept more than half of India's trade for itself; the rest was mainly with countries such as China, Ceylon and Persia. India usually ran an export surplus, not an import surplus.

questions.stem_md: The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 affected India's trade mainly by

options.text_md: diverting all Indian trade to China
cutting the cost and time of shipping between Britain and India, tightening British control of trade
ending India's exports of raw materials
making Indian handicrafts competitive again

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** cutting the cost and time of shipping between Britain and India, tightening British control of trade. The canal shortened the sea route between Britain and India, so British goods reached India faster and more cheaply and raw materials flowed out more easily. It did not divert trade to China, end raw-material exports or revive crafts.

questions.stem_md: India's large export surplus under colonial rule did **not** build up its wealth because

options.text_md: it was spent on building heavy industries in India
exports were always smaller than imports
it was invested in Indian schools and hospitals
it was used to pay for the colonial government's expenses in Britain, wars and invisible imports

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** it was used to pay for the colonial government's expenses in Britain, wars and invisible imports. The surplus went out of the country as payments for the colonial establishment in Britain, war expenses and services such as shipping: a drain of wealth. It was not used for Indian industry or welfare, and exports did exceed imports.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Despite an export surplus, colonial India faced shortages of essential goods such as food grains, clothes and kerosene.

**Reason (R):** The export surplus was drained out to meet the expenses of the colonial administration and was not used to import goods India needed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since the surplus left the country, it did not pay for imports of necessities or bring in gold, so shortages persisted alongside a surplus.

questions.stem_md: The ___ Canal, opened in 1869, became a highway for trade between Britain and India.
questions.solution_md: The Suez Canal shortened the route and lowered the cost of British trade with India.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined year, colonial India's exports were worth ₹380 crore and its imports ₹290 crore. Calculate the export surplus.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Export surplus = exports − imports.
Step 2: 380 − 290 = 90. So ₹90 crore.

questions.stem_md: Match each year with the event linked to it in the economic history of colonial India.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Railways began carrying passengers in 1853; the Suez Canal opened in 1869; the first census was taken in 1881; TISCO was incorporated in 1907.

questions.stem_md: State two features of India's foreign trade during colonial rule.
questions.solution_md: Any two of composition, direction, export surplus and its drain.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Composition:** India **exported raw materials** (cotton, jute, silk, indigo) and **imported finished goods** (cloth, light machinery).
2. **Direction:** Britain held a **monopoly**: more than half of the trade was with Britain.

questions.stem_md: India had an export surplus throughout colonial rule. Why is it said that this surplus was a "drain" rather than a gain?
questions.solution_md: Where the surplus went, what India failed to receive, and the effect on people.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The surplus was **used up abroad**: it paid for the **colonial administration in Britain**, its **wars** and services such as shipping and insurance.
2. **No gold or silver** flowed into India in return, so the surplus did not add to national wealth.
3. Meanwhile India faced **shortages of food grains, cloth and kerosene**, so the people gained nothing from it.

questions.stem_md: Explain how colonial policy shaped the composition, direction and outcome of India's foreign trade.
questions.solution_md: Composition, direction, Suez, surplus and drain, and the outcome.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Composition:** India became an **exporter of primary products** (raw cotton, silk, jute, indigo, sugar) and an **importer of finished consumer goods** and light machinery.
2. **Direction:** Britain controlled trade, so **more than half** of it was with Britain; the rest went mainly to China, Ceylon and Persia.
3. **Suez Canal (1869):** cheaper, faster shipping tightened this pattern.
4. **Export surplus:** exports exceeded imports, but the surplus paid for the **colonial establishment, wars and invisible imports**: a **drain** of wealth.
5. **Outcome:** shortages of grain, cloth and kerosene at home, and no foundation for Indian industry.

questions.stem_md: The first official census of British India was taken in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1881. The census series began in 1881. 1921 marks the demographic divide; 1853 and 1907 relate to railways and TISCO.

questions.stem_md: Why is 1921 called the year of the **great divide** in India's demographic history?

options.text_md: After 1921 the population began to fall every decade
It was the year of India's first census
After 1921 the population grew steadily, as India moved into the second stage of the demographic transition
Birth and death rates both became low in 1921

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** After 1921 the population grew steadily, as India moved into the second stage of the demographic transition. Before 1921 growth was uneven and slow; after it the death rate fell while the birth rate stayed high, so population grew steadily (the second stage). The first census was in 1881, and low birth and death rates came much later.

questions.stem_md: An imagined region has a birth rate of 46 and a death rate of 44 per thousand people per year. Its population

options.text_md: grows very fast, as in the second stage
falls quickly every year
grows very slowly, as in the first stage of the demographic transition
is in the final stage of low birth and death rates

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** grows very slowly, as in the first stage of the demographic transition. With both rates high and close together, natural growth is only about 2 per thousand a year: slow growth, typical of the first stage (India before 1921). Fast growth needs a falling death rate with a high birth rate.

questions.stem_md: On the eve of independence, the overall literacy rate in India was roughly

options.text_md: less than 16 per cent
about 50 per cent
about 75 per cent
about 90 per cent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** less than 16 per cent. Fewer than one in six people could read and write; female literacy was far lower, at about 7 per cent. The higher figures belong to much later decades.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Life expectancy in colonial India was very low, at about 32 years.

**Reason (R):** Public health facilities were scarce, and water-borne and air-borne diseases spread widely.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: with little public health care, diseases and famines caused high death rates, including very high infant mortality, so average life was short.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Before 1921, India's population grew rapidly because the death rate had fallen sharply.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The opposite: before 1921 both birth and death rates were high, so growth was slow and uneven. Steady growth came after 1921, when the death rate began to fall.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined district of 1941, 2,400 out of 15,000 people could read and write. Calculate its literacy rate.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Literacy rate = literates ÷ population × 100.
Step 2: 2,400 ÷ 15,000 × 100 = 16 per cent, close to the all-India level of the time.

questions.stem_md: If the infant mortality rate was 218 per thousand live births, how many of 5,000 babies born in an imagined district would be expected to die before their first birthday?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Deaths = rate ÷ 1,000 × births.
Step 2: 218 ÷ 1000 × 5,000 = 1,090 infants.

questions.stem_md: Describe any two demographic features of India on the eve of independence.
questions.solution_md: Any two: high vital rates, high infant mortality, low literacy, low life expectancy, poverty.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **High birth and death rates:** until 1921 population grew slowly; **infant mortality** was over 200 per thousand.
2. **Low quality of life:** **literacy** was below 16 per cent and **life expectancy** was only about 32 years.

questions.stem_md: How did the demographic condition of colonial India reflect its economic backwardness? Give three points.
questions.solution_md: Three indicators, each tied to an economic cause or effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Short lives:** life expectancy of about **32 years** showed poor nutrition and **scarce public health** care.
2. **High infant mortality** (over 200 per thousand) showed the absence of clean water and medical help in villages.
3. **Low literacy** (under 16 per cent, about 7 per cent for women) showed **neglect of education**, which kept productivity and incomes low.

marking_scheme.step: Life expectancy linked to health care
Infant mortality linked to living conditions

questions.stem_md: On the eve of independence, about what share of India's workforce was engaged in agriculture?

options.text_md: 30 to 35 per cent
10 to 15 per cent
90 to 95 per cent
70 to 75 per cent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 70 to 75 per cent. Agriculture employed roughly 70–75 per cent of workers, with manufacturing about 10 per cent and services about 15–20 per cent.

questions.stem_md: What does it show that in some regions (parts of the Madras, Bombay and Bengal presidencies) the share of agriculture in the workforce fell slightly, while in others (such as Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab) it rose?

options.text_md: A rapid all-India shift of workers into factories
Growing regional variation in occupational structure
That agriculture had become highly productive everywhere
That services employed most workers in every province

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Growing regional variation in occupational structure. The changes went in opposite directions in different areas, so the main lesson is unevenness between regions. There was no rapid national shift to industry, no general rise in farm productivity, and services were a minor employer.

questions.stem_md: An imagined province in 1946 had 2,50,000 workers, of whom 1,80,000 worked in agriculture. What percentage of its workforce was in agriculture?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Share = agricultural workers ÷ all workers × 100.
Step 2: 1,80,000 ÷ 2,50,000 × 100 = 72 per cent.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the three sectors in **descending** order of their share in India's workforce on the eve of independence.

options.text_md: Agriculture (primary sector)
Manufacturing (secondary sector)
Services (tertiary sector)

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (a) → (c) → (b). Agriculture had about 70–75 per cent, services about 15–20 per cent and manufacturing about 10 per cent.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What is meant by occupational structure? Describe India's occupational structure in 1947.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus the three approximate shares.

answer.model_answer_md: **Occupational structure** is the distribution of the **workforce among sectors**. In 1947 about **70–75 per cent** worked in **agriculture**, about **10 per cent** in **manufacturing** and about **15–20 per cent** in **services**.

questions.stem_md: The first passenger train in India ran in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1853. Passenger rail service began in 1853. The other years mark the Suez Canal, the first census and TISCO.

questions.stem_md: Which was a **positive** effect of the railways in colonial India?

options.text_md: They raised the incomes of most cultivators
They enabled long-distance travel and helped break geographical and cultural barriers
They protected Indian handicrafts from foreign competition
They ended famines in India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They enabled long-distance travel and helped break geographical and cultural barriers. Railways let people travel far and mix across regions. They did not raise most farmers' incomes, they actually carried cheap British goods into the interior (hurting crafts), and famines still occurred.

questions.stem_md: Roads, railways, ports and the telegraph were developed under colonial rule mainly to

options.text_md: connect every village to markets for the benefit of farmers
build a national industrial base for Indian entrepreneurs
move troops and administer the colony, and carry raw materials to ports and British goods inland
promote tourism within India

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** move troops and administer the colony, and carry raw materials to ports and British goods inland. The network served colonial purposes: administration, defence and an export-oriented trade. Most villages stayed unconnected, it was not meant to help Indian industry, and tourism was not the aim.

questions.stem_md: A colonial official in Lahore (imagined scene) sends an urgent message to Calcutta about unrest. Which colonial-era infrastructure best served this purpose?

options.text_md: Inland waterways
Public schools
Village wells
The electric telegraph

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The electric telegraph. The electric telegraph was expanded largely to keep law and order and speed up administrative messages. Waterways carry goods slowly, and schools and wells do not carry messages.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Railways helped the commercialisation of Indian agriculture.

**Reason (R):** Railways allowed people to travel long distances and broke down cultural barriers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is true: railways carried cash crops to ports and widened markets. R is also true, but it describes a social effect; it does not explain the spread of cash crops.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Some inland waterways developed in colonial times, such as a coastal canal in Orissa, proved uneconomical and could not compete with the railways.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Waterways like the Orissa coastal canal were expensive to run and lost traffic to the railways that ran alongside them.

questions.stem_md: Match each part of colonial infrastructure with the colonial purpose it mainly served.

options.text_md: Railways
Electric telegraph
Ports
Roads to the frontier

match_right.text_md: Handling the export–import trade with Britain
Carrying raw materials to ports and British goods inland

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Railways moved goods for trade; the telegraph sped up messages for law and order; ports handled overseas trade; roads served military movement.

questions.stem_md: Give one positive and one negative effect of the railways in colonial India.
questions.solution_md: One benefit and one cost, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Positive:** long-distance travel became possible, breaking **geographical and cultural barriers** and widening markets.
**Negative:** they carried **cheap British goods** into the interior and raw materials out, which **hurt handicrafts** and served export trade more than Indians.

questions.stem_md: Explain why infrastructure developed under colonial rule did not serve the needs of the Indian people.
questions.solution_md: Purpose, coverage and effects, each tied to people's needs.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Purpose:** railways, roads and ports were built to **move troops**, run the administration and serve **export trade**, not to link villages.
2. **Coverage:** most rural areas lacked **all-weather roads**, so farmers could not reach markets, especially in the rains.
3. **Effects:** the network carried **British goods inland**, hurting crafts, and the costly **telegraph** served law and order more than commerce of ordinary people.

questions.stem_md: "Colonial infrastructure was a mixed blessing for India." Evaluate this statement.
questions.solution_md: Two benefits, two limitations, and a reasoned judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Railways (from 1853):** allowed **long-distance travel**, broke geographical and cultural barriers and widened markets.
2. **Communications:** posts and the **electric telegraph** linked distant parts of the country.
3. **But the purpose was colonial:** routes connected the interior to **ports**, moving raw materials out and **British goods in**, which hurt handicrafts.
4. **Uneven coverage:** most **villages lacked all-weather roads**; some waterways, like a coastal canal in Orissa, proved uneconomical.
5. **Judgement:** the network gave independent India a **useful base**, but it was built for **administration and trade**, not for the people's development, so it was indeed a mixed blessing.

marking_scheme.step: Colonial purpose and effect on crafts

questions.stem_md: Which combination best sums up the Indian economy in 1947?

options.text_md: Modern agriculture, strong heavy industry and a large import surplus
High literacy, long life expectancy and a large service sector
Rapid growth in output per head and full employment
Stagnant agriculture, weak industry, export-oriented trade, poor health and education, limited infrastructure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Stagnant agriculture, weak industry, export-oriented trade, poor health and education, limited infrastructure. At independence the economy showed all the colonial weaknesses: stagnant farms, a narrow industrial base, trade geared to Britain, low literacy and life expectancy, and infrastructure built for colonial needs.

questions.stem_md: Which three challenges did the colonial legacy leave for the planners of independent India?
questions.solution_md: Three challenges, each linked to a colonial weakness.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Agriculture:** raising **farm productivity** through land reform, irrigation and new technology.
2. **Industry:** building a **capital goods** base and creating jobs for those displaced by de-industrialisation.
3. **People:** tackling **poverty, illiteracy and poor health**, and extending infrastructure to **villages**.

questions.stem_md: Critically appraise the impact of British rule on the Indian economy, giving one point each on agriculture, industry, foreign trade, demography and infrastructure.
questions.solution_md: One supported point per area and an overall conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Agriculture:** stagnant; **zamindari** rent, little irrigation or technology; commercialisation helped traders more than tillers.
2. **Industry:** **de-industrialisation** of handicrafts; only a few cotton and jute mills, TISCO, and **no capital goods** base.
3. **Foreign trade:** India exported **raw materials** and imported finished goods; Britain's **monopoly**; the export surplus was **drained** away.
4. **Demography:** high birth and death rates, life expectancy about **32 years**, literacy under **16 per cent**.
5. **Infrastructure:** railways, ports and the telegraph built mainly for **colonial purposes**, though they later proved a useful base. Overall, the economy was left **poor and stagnant**.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined letter written by SOYL for practice; the people and village are not real.)*

**(b)** A shift to a cash crop sold to mills shows commercialisation.

**OR (c) (ii)** Show how transport carried imported cloth into the interior.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.passage_md:
**Letter from Haripada, a weaver of an imagined village near Dhaka, to his brother in Calcutta, 1885**

Dear Dada, our looms are mostly silent now. The merchant who once bought our fine cloth says the city people want the cheap printed cloth that comes by ship from England and by train to our market town. Father has rented a small plot from the zamindar's agent to grow jute, which the agent says the Calcutta mills will buy. But the rent is high, the rains failed last year, and we still owe the moneylender. Cousin Nitai has gone to look for work at the jute mill near your quarters. Send news if there is any work there for me too.

children.stem_md: Name the process shown by the "silent looms" of the weavers.
children.solution_md: Handloom weaving collapsing under machine-made imports is de-industrialisation.

answer.model_answer_md: **De-industrialisation** (decline of handicrafts).

children.stem_md: Which feature of colonial agriculture is shown by the father growing jute for the mills?
children.solution_md: A shift to a cash crop sold to mills shows commercialisation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Commercialisation of agriculture**: growing a cash crop for industry instead of food.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Identify two problems in the letter that kept the family poor even after the switch to jute.
children.solution_md: Pick two obstacles from the passage and link each to poverty.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **High rent** to the zamindar's agent took most of the earnings. (2) **Dependence on rain** (no irrigation) and **debt** to the moneylender left them exposed when the crop failed.

Second problem with link to poverty

marking_scheme.step: Railways carried it inland, displacing local cloth

questions.stem_md: Study the table and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined province and rounded figures, written by SOYL for practice; the all-India column gives commonly cited approximate shares.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Step 1: Share = service workers ÷ total × 100.
Step 2: 45,000 ÷ 2,50,000 × 100 = 18 per cent.

**(b)** Compare the province's shares with the all-India column.

**(c) (i)** Link the share to the weakness of industry and to low incomes.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two reasons linked to de-industrialisation and lack of alternatives.
